paragraphs: Friend, here's what this psalm teaches me: you can bring God the whole mess. David doesn't clean it up first. He opens with "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1), and he says it straight to God, not about Him. Honest cries belong in prayer, and this psalm proves it.

Now look at the two little words that keep turning David around. "Yet You are holy" (Psalm 22:3). "Yet You brought me forth from the womb" (Psalm 22:9). He doesn't pretend the trouble isn't there, but he keeps remembering who God has always been. I do the same thing when the oven's acting up and I still say, "This oven has never let me down before." Remembering isn't ignoring the pain, friend. It's where hope starts to stand back up.

And then the whole psalm swings. David goes from feeling like "a worm and not a man" (Psalm 22:6) to praising in the great assembly, because "He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help" (Psalm 22:24). It doesn't stay with David either. It grows until the ends of the earth turn to the LORD and a people yet unborn hear about "all that He has done" (Psalm 22:27, 31). So when your night feels long, friend, cry out honestly, remember who God is, and keep your ovens ready for what comes next.
